exam-14-q01.why_correct_en: St Patrick's Day is celebrated on 17 March because tradition holds that St Patrick died on that date in the fifth century, so the Church observed it as his feast day; it is not his birthday. His exact birth and death dates are not established by contemporary records, so 17 March is best understood as a long-standing tradition rather than a fully documented date. Patrick was probably born in Roman Britain, was abducted to Ireland when young, escaped and trained as a cleric, then returned to spread Christianity. For the test he is associated with Northern Ireland; more broadly, he is the patron saint of Ireland.

exam-14-q02.why_correct_en: The Northern Ireland Assembly uses a proportional system called the Single Transferable Vote (STV). Northern Ireland has 18 constituencies, each returning five MLAs, for 90 in total. Rather than marking an X for one candidate, voters rank candidates 1, 2, 3 and so on. A quota is calculated by dividing valid votes by the number of seats plus one, taking the whole number, then adding one. Candidates who reach it are elected; surplus votes transfer according to later preferences. If nobody reaches the quota, the lowest candidate is eliminated and those ballots transfer. This repeats until all seats are filled, allowing representation to reflect support more proportionately.

exam-14-q07.why_correct_en: Hogmanay is Scotland's name for New Year's Eve and its New Year celebration, beginning on 31 December and continuing into New Year's Day. Traditions include singing Robert Burns's Auld Lang Syne at midnight, fireworks and torchlight, and first-footing: the first visitor after midnight brings gifts such as coal, shortbread or whisky, symbolising warmth, food and good cheer. Hogmanay became especially important after the Scottish Reformation, when the Kirk discouraged Catholic-associated Christmas festivities and the Scottish Parliament prohibited the Yule vacation in 1640. Christmas did not become a Scottish public holiday until 1958. The origin of the word Hogmanay remains uncertain.

exam-14-q12.why_correct_en: The correct answer is the Crimean War (1853–56). Rising literacy, cheaper printing and railway distribution expanded newspaper readership, while the telegraph accelerated reports. The Times correspondent William Howard Russell accompanied the army and reported disease, cold, poor supplies and hospital conditions directly to readers. In 1855 Roger Fenton took a camera and mobile darkroom to Crimea and systematically photographed soldiers, camps and the landscape. It is therefore commonly described as the first major conflict extensively covered by modern war correspondents and systematic photography. Long exposures and bulky equipment prevented photographs of combat in progress, and newspapers often reproduced photographs as engravings rather than printing them directly.
